# Filtering your search by file type

You often want to search only one kind of file, and leave the rest alone.
ripgrep knows how, and you don't have to spell out file extensions to tell it.
It ships with names for common file types, and four flags let you use those
names, see them, and invent your own.

By default ripgrep searches the current directory and everything below it, so
a type filter is usually how you tell it which of those files you care about.
Add the filter to any search you already run; nothing else about the command
changes.

## Search only one type: `-t/--type`

Say you keep your work in Markdown and you want every line that mentions
`draft`:

```
$ rg draft --type md
```

or, more briefly:

```
$ rg draft -tmd
```

The `-t` flag acts as a name for one or more file-name patterns. The name `md`
stands for `*.md`, `*.markdown`, and a few more, so you match all of them at
once instead of listing each. You can pass `-t` more than once to search
several types together:

```
$ rg draft -tmd -thtml
```

That searches Markdown and HTML files, and nothing else.

## Skip a type: `-T/--type-not`

The mirror image. `-t` means "include files of this type"; `-T` means "exclude
files of this type." To search everything except HTML:

```
$ rg copyright --type-not html
```

or:

```
$ rg copyright -Thtml
```

You can stack `-T`, and you can mix it with `-t`. Excluding one noisy type is
often the quickest way to clear clutter out of your results.

## See what's available: `--type-list`

ripgrep comes with names for a couple hundred file types, so before you guess,
ask:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line: the name, a colon, then the comma-separated
file-name patterns it stands for. To find just one, search the list with
ripgrep itself:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^txt:'
txt: *.txt
```

Some types answer to more than one name. Markdown, for instance, is both `md`
and `markdown`, so `-tmd` and `-tmarkdown` do the same thing. The list is the
place to check when a name doesn't behave the way you expected, or when you're
not sure a type exists at all.

## Make your own: `--type-add`

If your files don't fit a built-in name, define one. Suppose you think of
Markdown and plain text together as your "notes":

```
$ rg heading --type-add 'notes:*.md' --type-add 'notes:*.txt' -tnotes
```

One pattern per `--type-add`, but you can pass the flag as many times as you
like. There's a shorthand for several extensions at once:

```
$ rg heading --type-add 'notes:*.{md,txt}' -tnotes
```

You can also build a new type out of types that already exist, with the special
`include` directive:

```
$ rg heading --type-add 'notes:include:md,txt,html' -tnotes
```

That pulls in every pattern already defined for `md`, `txt`, and `html`. Type
names must be letters or numbers only. Punctuation isn't allowed.

One thing to know: `--type-add` lasts only for the command you run it in.
ripgrep doesn't save it anywhere. If you want `notes` available every day,
either make a shell alias:

```
$ alias rg="rg --type-add 'notes:*.{md,txt,html}'"
```

or put the same `--type-add` line in your ripgrep configuration file, so every
search starts with it.

## The special name `all`

`--type all` searches every file ripgrep recognizes, and nothing it doesn't.
It works as a whitelist: if a file matches no known type, it's skipped. That's
handy when you want to steer clear of files ripgrep has no name for at all.

`--type-not all` is the reverse. It searches only the files ripgrep does not
recognize.

One catch is worth knowing. Types match on the file name, so a file with no
extension belongs to no type. A note simply named `notes`, with no extension,
won't be found by `--type all`, though `notes.txt` will. And `--type-not all`
would find `notes` but skip `notes.txt`.

## When a file you expected doesn't appear

The `-t` flag has lower precedence than two other things: the `-g/--glob` flag,
and the rules in ignore files such as `.gitignore`. So an explicit glob or an
ignore rule can still keep a file out of your results even when its type
matches. If a file you expected is missing, that's the first place to look.

That's the whole of it. `-t` includes a type, `-T` excludes one, `--type-list`
shows you the names, and `--type-add` lets you coin your own for the length of a
command. Reach for the built-in names first; you'll be surprised how many are
already there.
